lines.text: The Skeld trails run along the edge of the White, where nothing lives that wants to be found. Garrow led. Wren drove.
Up. Again. We stop when we're dead, and not before.
Oswin carried Nell on his back, wrapped in his torn blue cloak. His wounds opened on the first day. He didn't mention it. His thread did.
I was a steward, my lord. Stewards don't climb. Stewards sit, and write things down.
Then sit on that rock and write down that you're getting up.
Wherever I walked, the snow melted into a black path behind me. Garrow said the Skeld would be able to follow it for a year.
On the second night, the threads from home grew loud. Hundreds of them, frightened, tugging at me like children at a sleeve.
On the third morning, the first of them went sharp. Then a dozen more. The siege had begun.
That afternoon, there were riders behind us. Hounds, with dogs, following my black path through the snow. Caddoc had sent them north the day he took my father.
There's an ice bridge over the gorge ahead. Old as the Skeld. It holds four at a time. Go. Now.
We crossed in twos and threes, over a span of white ice no wider than a cart, above a drop with no bottom.
Wren and Garrow crossed last. Halfway over, they stopped, turned round, and drew.
Father and daughter. Same stance, same red-thread arrows, same way of holding their breath. Nine Hounds came onto the bridge. Not one of them reached the middle.
Now, girl. The keystone.
Wren put an arrow into the old ice at the centre of the span, where the Skeld had always said it would break. It broke.
They ran the last ten paces on falling ice, and landed in the snow beside us, laughing like idiots.
You held that bridge like a man half your age, old man.
I held it like a man with his daughter behind him. It's different.
I didn't know it yet, but I had just watched two commoners hold a bridge for the realm.
After that, Wren pushed us past breaking. Then she pushed us past that, too.
On the fourth night, we came over the last ridge, and saw Greyhollow.
Three thousand campfires lay in the snow around it, like a noose around a throat. And on the wall above the gate stood one small figure, with one arm.
The Lord Who Measured Zero. Chapter one hundred and seventeen, coming soon.
